contentSections: In most of India, the sun is not a guest, it is the main design problem. A west wall in Delhi in May, an unshaded glass front in Ahmedabad, a south facing office in Hyderabad: each one turns into a heat trap that your air conditioning has to fight all day. A solar shading facade stops sunlight before it reaches the glass or wall, so the heat never enters. This guide explains how shading works, compares fins, louvers and screens, and helps you choose the right system for your building.

Why Shade the Facade, Not Just the Room?

Blinds and curtains inside a room block light, but the heat has already entered the building. Shading on the outside stops the heat at the source. That is why external shading is one of the most effective ways to reduce cooling load, glare and discomfort. Good solar shading can:

• Reduce heat gain through glass and walls
  • Lower air conditioning load and energy use
  • Cut glare on screens and workspaces
  • Keep daylight while blocking direct sun
  • Give the building a distinct visual identity

Know Your Sun Before You Choose a System

Shading design starts with orientation, because the sun hits each side differently.

OrientationSun behaviourBest shading approach
NorthLow direct sun in most of IndiaLight shading or none
EastLow morning sun at a steep side angleVertical fins
SouthHigh sun in summer, lower in winterHorizontal projections, louvers
WestLow, hot afternoon sunVertical fins, dense screens, or both
For more on this, see our guide on facade options for south facing homes. West faces need special attention, and we cover them in a separate guide.
5 Shading Systems Compared

1. Vertical Fins

Tall blades placed side by side, fixed at an angle. They work best on east and west faces, where the sun comes in low from the side. Fins also give a strong vertical rhythm to a building. Our guide on architectural fins design shows how one element can define a facade, and the MetaFin system is built for this purpose.

2. Horizontal Louvers and Brise Soleil

Horizontal blades block high sun from above, which suits south facing walls and windows. Spacing and depth are set by the sun angle you want to cut. See the MetaLouver range for louver options.

3. Perforated Metal Screens

A perforated panel filters light through holes of a chosen size and pattern. It cuts heat and glare while keeping some view and airflow, and creates beautiful patterns of light and shadow. Read more in our article on the power of perforation.

4. Expanded Mesh and Woven Screens

Light, flexible screens that hang a short distance off the facade. They soften sun and add texture, and suit parking, staircases and double skin facades.

5. Movable and Adjustable Shading

Fins or louvers that rotate or slide change their angle through the day or season. They give more control but need motors, controls and upkeep, so use them where the benefit justifies the cost.
Fixed vs Adjustable Shading

FactorFixed shadingAdjustable shading
CostLowerHigher
UpkeepVery lowRegular servicing
ControlSet by designChanges with conditions
ReliabilityHigh, no moving partsDepends on mechanism
Best forMost Indian projectsShowpiece and high performance buildings
For most buildings, a well designed fixed system gives the best balance of performance and simplicity.
Design Details That Make Shading Work

• Depth and spacing. Deeper blades block more sun but also more view and light. Set depth by the sun angle for your latitude.
  • Blade angle. A slight tilt can block direct sun while letting diffuse daylight in.
  • Distance from the wall. A gap lets hot air escape instead of trapping it behind the screen.
  • Colour and finish. Light colours reflect more heat. Quality finishes keep their colour in strong sun.
  • Structure and wind load. Large shading elements catch wind, so fixings and sub-frames must be designed for it.
  • Cleaning access. Plan for safe cleaning of both sides of the shading.
Natural airflow behind the screen is a big benefit. Our article on ventilated metal facade systems explains how this works.

Light and Shadow as a Design Tool

Shading does not have to be plain. The interplay of light and shadow through fins and screens changes through the day and makes the facade feel alive. We go deeper in the science of light and shadow in metal facade design.

Choosing the Right Material

Aluminium is the most common material for shading elements because it is light, resists corrosion and takes many finishes. Steel suits heavy duty or long span elements and needs proper coating. Whatever you choose, ask for finish and warranty details. See our guide on facade materials compared.

Green Building Benefits

Shading lowers energy use, which supports green building goals. Read how sustainability goals influence metal panel selection for more on this link.
Common Mistakes

• Using the same shading on every side of the building
  • Choosing looks over sun angle
  • Blocking too much daylight, which raises lighting use
  • Forgetting wind load on large screens
  • Ignoring cleaning and upkeep access
Frequently Asked Questions

Does external shading really reduce AC bills?

Yes. Stopping sun before it reaches glass or walls cuts heat gain, which reduces cooling load. The saving depends on orientation, glass area and the shading design.

Which shading is best for west facing walls?

Vertical fins, dense perforated screens or a combination, since the sun is low and hot in the afternoon.

Are fixed or adjustable fins better?

Fixed fins are simpler and need almost no upkeep. Adjustable fins give more control but cost more and need servicing.

Will shading block my view?

Good design keeps views by controlling blade depth, angle and spacing, or by using perforated or mesh screens.

Which material is best for shading fins?

Aluminium is the most popular choice because of its light weight, corrosion resistance and finish options.
